Tuli Elephant man Craig Saunders at it again with animal sanctuary in a wetland

By: Liz Fish | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
Controversial businessman and owner of 3 elephant Sanctuaries Craig Saunders is applying to open a 4th facility in the Western Cape just outside Kleinmond called Lamlock Animal Sanctuary. He plans to bring 6 elephants, 3 Rhino and various buck onto a farm that incorporates a massive wetland system. Despite huge public opposition to development on this wetland and an extensive EIA which appears to have been halted it appears the permits for 2 Elephants from his Hazyview property are in the final stages of being granted. Part of the opposition is that he has re-established a fence through the wetland initially trapping the herd of wild horses and other wild animals that move freely through the area
Craig Saunders was originally charged for animal cruelty for his part in the abuse of the Tuli Elephant saga but charges were later dropped for insufficient evidence. He bought 5 of the Thuli elephants which witnesses said he beat about the head with a stick. Due to mounting international pressure only recently Saunders has stopped elephant back rides in his Hartbeespoort facility.
Currently there are containers bordering an small enclosed area on land that has been cleared of aliens. The initial application was that the elephant would be enclosed in this area where visitors could view them, controlled by their elephant handlers and then the elephants would be able to wander through the wetland.
Currently the EMS Foundation have engaged their lawyers to get the Department of Environmental affairs land use to concluded the EIA on the land but will Saunders be able to circumvent this through other legislation and move animals?

Script:


Script: Just an hour's drive from Cape Town, there is an exquisite wetland system that stretches between the Bot river and Kleinmond Estuary, a critically endangered ecosystem. It’s one of seven estuarine lakes in the country with over 250 bird species and a herd of wild horses, and right in the middle, lies Lamloch farm. Craig Saunders bought the farm 7 years ago with a dream to create the Kleinmond Wildlife Sanctuary, bringing in his elephants from his other facilities. But it’s causing major strife in both conservation, and elephant circles.
Michele “He needs to let them go and let him be in the wild with other elephants in places where elephants actually normally wander around . Kleinmond with not a tree in sight is not a place for elephants.
Script: Michele Pickover director of EMS Foundation, a social justice NGO, wants the 95 elephants in captivity in South Africa rewilded. Saunders has 12 elephants in 3 sanctuaries, Hazyview, Haartbeespoort and Plettenbergbay. These elephants have been ridden up until recently, and they still perform tricks daily for tourists.

Michele: people don't understand that when they go to the elephant back safari places,and they feed an elephant or they interact with an elephant or they ride an elephant. They don't understand what that elephant has been through how its spirit has been broken to allow them to do that.
Upsound “This footage is Saunders in 1999. “ Script: “ The Tuli saga still casts a shadow in Saunders' life. Carte Blanche broadcast this footage which appeared to show him abusing baby elephants while working as a volunteer at Riccardo Ghiazza’s facility. They were training the captured Tuli baby elephants for export to Zoo’s overseas.
Derek: You were charged with animal abuse at the time. Any regrets about your involvement with the Tuli elephants.
Craig “We were acquitted on the first day that we actually that evidence was led at the trial .There was no intention ever of mine to actually inflict or be cruel on on any level to this day I maintain my innocence in it
Script: Saunders said he never witnessed or took part in the brutal beatings, and the state could not prove their case. He went on to buy five of the baby Tuli elephants from a different location, which he trained for elephant back rides, and they’ve spent the last twenty years working in his sanctuaries. Like Kumba, taken from the wild as a baby, she goes down on her knees for you to pop the question. It’s activities like these that make people suspicious of Saunders intentions for the new Sanctuary.

Michele: Look let's get this right, this is not a sanctuary, it’s the opposite of a sanctuary. This is a business
LINK “Craig Saunders has had an elephant management plan approved to bring six of the animals here to his property in Kleinmond despite the fact that elephants haven’t roamed freely here since the early 1700s
Craig “When we came here originally it reminded me a bit of Botswana out on the delta and elephants were here before I mean there is huge amounts of elephant paths in the back of Hermanus which are historically well documented. So the elephants were here

Script: Rob Fryer of Whale Coast Conservation is extremely concerned about the destruction he says elephants will cause in this threatened wetland system
Rob: there are claims by Craig Saunders that elephants used to frequent this area. They may well have done passing through but they wouldn't have been residing in such a small area for any length of time.
Script: Having initially considered breeding buffalo, keeping lions, rhino, and hippo, Saunders adapted his ideas and currently Eland, zebra, bontebok and springbok are on the property
Then early in 2019 he set the cat among the pigeons with an environmental impact assessment for an ambitious safari park, which included a tented camp on stilts in the vlei , 20 chalets, a manor house and restaurant. Extensive objections were lodged, and in the interim, Saunders has changed his plans.
Rob: there are many areas that are not environmentally sensitive in close proximity to Cape Town that could have been used for this tourist attraction. Why do it in a highly sensitive, in crisis according to the biodiversity assessment area such as this
Script: EMS wanted to see the Elephant management plan before CapeNature granted the permits. But Dr Ernst Baart of CapeNature explained that Saunders had a right to withhold them, which he did.

Derek: if he doesn't build overnight accommodation, he doesn't have to have an EIA and he's won the War.

Ernst: the footprint that is on that property right now it does not trigger any of the EIA regulations and therefore he is technically not in breach of the National Environmental Management Act, it's as simple as that.
Derek: The claim is that you've successfully avoided public participation as to what happens in this highly sensitive area.
Craig” The wildlife applications is handled by the agency of CapeNature that is not a public participation process . So just as a farmer would decide what animals he wants to keep he goes then through the necessary legislation through the necessary agencies and he then actually puts together or he applies for permits based on what he intends to keep
Link: Human animal interactions have become internationally frowned upon in recent years, SA Tourism wants them banned and there are particular sensitivities when it comes to elephants
Derek: Michele you get elephant back rides you get to walk with them which elements are you against

Michele: Absolutely every single one of them. We should not be doing anything with elephants unless we actually try to help them in a situation in the wild where they might be snared or something like that.

Derek: it's claimed that there is a degree of cruelty involved in any elephant human interaction would you agree
Saunders: This become a new rhetoric and a new conversation saying that all elephants training or familiarization involves cruelty and I don't believe that for a second
Derek: what interactions will you offer to the public here.
Saunders: There won't be any interactions.
Derek: No riding
Saunders: no riding no interactions no touching.
Derek: So what will the public do.
Craig “The product has changed extensively over the last six years. So what will they do now, they do a game drive they will do a game walk, there is a magnificent birding opportunities here and the fynbos is here
Derek: So isn't this a costly venture out of step with modern times.
Saunders: Yes it is a costly venture but you know ultimately we've decided how we want to go into the next phase of our lives. And this is a unique opportunity that the elephant to have more time and more space.

Michele to take two elephants put them on a piece of land that hasn't a tree in sight and then say well you know I'm not going to ride them, so I'm actually doing them a big favour and maybe retiring them. I mean it's very disingenuous

Derek: Organizations like the EMS Foundation say you've made your money from the elephants, it's time to release them into the true wild.
Saunders: No it's not what we say in not saying what's the true wild, where is the true wild Derek , where does it exist

Script: CapeNature say they have applied their minds to both the biodiversity concerns, and the welfare of the elephants, and although they don’t condone human interaction with wild animals, there is currently no legislation against it.
Ernst “We had the panel evaluate our evaluation of the elephants in Kleinmond at Lamloch and their unanimous support for bringing the elephants or allowing the animals gave us a level of comfort
Link: This sanctuary fence cuts right through the highly sensitive wetland and has caused a great deal of concern on many fronts
Derek: Rob the department says that this development doesn't contravene any coastal management regulations
Rob: there again you're taking a very legalistic view. There's every reason to extend the coastal public property boundary on this particular area to protect that area for posterity and to make sure that nothing happens there that can make an already critical system more in crisis system more vulnerable to degradation.
LINK “The wild horses of Kleinmond are rather mystical and largely unknown feature of the area they have roamed free for decades some would even say centuries
Script: Leanne Dryburgh is a horse watcher and one of the self appointed guardians of the 34 wild horses
Derek “ Leanne tell about the wild horses of Kleinmond
Leanne “There are a lot of romantic notions, the one is that they are from the Birkenhead shipwreck in 1852, the other is that they were left over from the Anglo Boer War. The most probable theory is this piece of land belonged to the Delports they bred mules and horses here and when tractors and things came in in the late 1950s he let his horses go, he no longer needed them.
Script: When Saunders closed the gates so he could release his game, the horses were trapped inside. By then the level of animosity was so high that within a week 23 000 people had signed a petition for the horses to be released, which Saunders did immediately.
Leanne “we can't stop a landowner from fencing off his land. But to be moved back from the vlei, if the fence just moved back off the water and the horses could just pass through like they have for many years I think there would be a fantastically happy relationship.
Saunders: There's a corridor of over a hundred meters between where the horses can move through, it doesn't stop the horses at all.
Script: And Capenature ensured he left gaps at the bottom of the fence to allow small animals to pass through. But Saunders says the horses re-seed the alien vegetation which he has painstakingly spent R6 million rands clearing off his property. And one thing everybody seems to agree upon, is that Saunders has done an incredible job, and he has had 12 different specialists looking at every angle.
Craig “If you drove through here previously there were just walls of port Jackson and walls of Australian myrtle straight through here they opened it up with a bulldozer that was the only way to get through

Script: Despite restoring the fynbos, Saunders is up against those who believe the space is too small for elephants. They will continue to fight to stop private landowners rights currently protected by outdated legislation. They believe it’s the public's right to protect the wetland and elephants in captivity.

Michele: We will go to the courts. We will go to the travel agents. We will insist that they understand that these businesses are a thing of the past

Script: Saunders has spent a great deal of time and money on his property and the elephant management plan has been approved. He’s applied for the transport permits for 2 elephants.
Craig “Our dream is we want elephant in this space , we want to have elephant rewilded in an area like this

Currently the EMS Foundation have engaged their lawyers to get the Department of Environmental affairs land use to concluded the EIA on the land but will Saunders be able to circumvent this through other legislation and move animals?
